title: Conrad Grebel

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Conrad Grebel belonged to the Zürich circle that sought a church ordered by the teaching and practice of the New Testament. On 21 January 1525, after prayer, he baptized George Blaurock upon his confession of faith. Blaurock then baptized the others who were present.
paragraphs: Conrad Grebel belonged to the Zürich circle that sought a church ordered by the teaching and practice of the New Testament. On 21 January 1525, after prayer, he baptized George Blaurock upon his confession of faith. Blaurock then baptized the others who were present.

The gathering joined baptism to a shared commitment to follow Christ and teach the gospel. Grebel therefore connects the Zürich event with the beginnings of the Swiss Brethren, alongside Felix Manz and Blaurock. The dated entry here identifies that gathering rather than the whole span of his life.

title: Felix Manz

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Felix Manz helped shape the early Zürich fellowship and shared its conviction that baptism should follow faith. Martyrs’ Mirror calls him Felix Mantz and describes his preaching, imprisonment, and death by drowning at Zürich.
paragraphs: Felix Manz helped shape the early Zürich fellowship and shared its conviction that baptism should follow faith. Martyrs’ Mirror calls him Felix Mantz and describes his preaching, imprisonment, and death by drowning at Zürich.

His preserved admonition gives a fuller picture of his convictions than the execution alone. He insists that Christian profession must bear the fruit of love and mercy, including love toward enemies, and rejects hatred and coercion as the work of Christ’s shepherds.

The original account prints 1526. This profile retains the separately cited 1527 date used in the Zürich overview, while linking directly to the unchanged account so both date statements remain visible.

title: George Blaurock

date.label: 1525–1529: baptism and ministry
date.basis: Zürich gathering in the cited MWC history; 1529 execution in Martyrs’ Mirror.

summary: George Blaurock asked Conrad Grebel to baptize him at the Zürich gathering of 21 January 1525 and then baptized the others present. The act expressed their commitment to become a fellowship of believers following Christ together.
paragraphs: George Blaurock asked Conrad Grebel to baptize him at the Zürich gathering of 21 January 1525 and then baptized the others present. The act expressed their commitment to become a fellowship of believers following Christ together.

Martyrs’ Mirror follows his preaching from Switzerland into Tyrol. Its 1529 account describes his arrest with companions and execution near Clausen, explaining that his rejection of infant baptism and the mass formed part of the charges. A separate admonition preserves the encouragement he left to those who would follow.

The same account tells how Jacob Huter served as a teacher in Tyrol and led people to Moravia amid persecution. That passage supplies a specific connection between the Swiss and Tyrolean stories and the communities later known as Hutterites.

title: Michael Sattler

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Michael Sattler is associated with the seven Schleitheim Articles of 1527, which address baptism, church discipline, the breaking of bread, separation, shepherds, the sword, and oaths. They set out a shared order of discipleship for the gathered brethren.
paragraphs: Michael Sattler is associated with the seven Schleitheim Articles of 1527, which address baptism, church discipline, the breaking of bread, separation, shepherds, the sword, and oaths. They set out a shared order of discipleship for the gathered brethren.

Martyrs’ Mirror preserves his trial as a sequence: the account of his hearing, the charges and answers, and a prison letter to the church at Horb. Reading these together shows how convictions about baptism and nonresistance became matters for which a believer could be condemned.

The prison letter carries the story beyond the courtroom. It exhorts the congregation to remain faithful to Christ, to live in obedience, and to hold together under pressure. These are linked here as parts of one documented account rather than as unrelated search matches.

paragraphs: Jakob Hutter led Anabaptist believers from Tyrol toward refuge in Moravia and helped organize their shared life. The Hutterite history dates his election as chief elder to 1533 and his execution at Innsbruck to 25 February 1536.

Martyrs’ Mirror uses the spelling Jacob Huter in its Blaurock account. It describes him as an overseer and teacher whose people joined the Moravian church as persecution increased. Its account of George Zaunringerad also records Huter’s part in placing a minister in service and sending him to Moravia.
These passages connect Hutter’s leadership to named people and movements within the book. Community of goods and the continuing Hutterite tradition are explored on the linked tradition page.

summary: Menno Simons was a former Dutch priest who became an influential Anabaptist teacher. The Mennonite name preserves his association with the communities he helped strengthen; it does not make every later branch the work of one founder.
paragraphs: Menno Simons was a former Dutch priest who became an influential Anabaptist teacher. The Mennonite name preserves his association with the communities he helped strengthen; it does not make every later branch the work of one founder.

A revealing passage in Martyrs’ Mirror occurs in Herman Vleckwijk’s prison disputation. Pressed about Menno and other teachers, Herman answers that his trust rests in God rather than in any man. The exchange shows both Menno’s public prominence and the believer’s insistence that Scripture and Christ stood above a teacher’s reputation.

summary: Dirk Willems was imprisoned at Asperen in Holland in 1569. Martyrs’ Mirror recounts that he escaped, crossed the ice, and turned back when the man pursuing him fell through it. His rescue of the pursuer cost him the opportunity to get away.
paragraphs: Dirk Willems was imprisoned at Asperen in Holland in 1569. Martyrs’ Mirror recounts that he escaped, crossed the ice, and turned back when the man pursuing him fell through it. His rescue of the pursuer cost him the opportunity to get away.

The officer was ordered to seize him again, and Dirk was subsequently condemned and executed. The account preserves the sentence as well as the rescue, allowing the reader to follow the action from imprisonment to judgment. The book’s illustration depicts him reaching toward the man in the water.

title: Anna Jans

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Anna Jans is the woman remembered in the supplied edition as Anna of Rotterdam. The account preserves the testament she gave to her son Isaiah on 24 January 1539, as she prepared to die for her faith.
paragraphs: Anna Jans is the woman remembered in the supplied edition as Anna of Rotterdam. The account preserves the testament she gave to her son Isaiah on 24 January 1539, as she prepared to die for her faith.

Her letter sets her suffering alongside that of Christ, the prophets, apostles, and earlier witnesses. She urges her son to follow the way of the Lord and seek the faithful, even when their fellowship is despised. Its many biblical references make the account both a mother’s farewell and an instruction in discipleship.

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Thieleman J. van Braght gathered the accounts, letters, confessions, and exhortations that make up Martyrs’ Mirror. He organized Christian witness century by century, bringing the testimony of the early church and medieval believers together with the sufferings of the Anabaptists.
paragraphs: Thieleman J. van Braght gathered the accounts, letters, confessions, and exhortations that make up Martyrs’ Mirror. He organized Christian witness century by century, bringing the testimony of the early church and medieval believers together with the sufferings of the Anabaptists.

His addresses to fellow believers make the collection a call to faithful discipleship. The valedictory is signed at Dort on 31 July 1659, and the address introducing the second part also bears his name and the year 1659. These authorial passages show his purpose in his own words, alongside the timeline’s 1660 publication milestone.

paragraphs: Stephen was one of the seven chosen to serve the church at Jerusalem. Martyrs’ Mirror follows Acts 6–7: his wisdom in dispute, the accusations against him, and his testimony before the council about God’s dealings with his people.

He was stoned outside the city, commending his spirit to the Lord and praying for those who killed him. The source heading assigns the event to 34. Its original illustration depicts the stoning and links the first-century chapter to a particular witness and place.

Martyrs’ Mirror’s separate account follows his suffering and gives his crucifixion under Nero the date 69. The narrative and its illustration lead from the apostolic preaching in Acts to the witness at Rome remembered by the book.

title: Ignatius of Antioch
paragraphs: Ignatius served the church at Antioch in Syria. Martyrs’ Mirror describes him as a disciple of John and a diligent shepherd whose teaching centered on Christ. Arrested under Trajan, he was sent under guard to Rome.

The journey became an opportunity to encourage other believers through letters. The account follows his steadfastness as he faced death by wild beasts, which its heading dates to 111. The accompanying illustration belongs to this account.

paragraphs: Blandina appears with Maturus, Sanctus, and a youth from Pontus among the Christians persecuted on the Rhône. Martyrs’ Mirror describes her confession of Christ as the source of her strength through repeated torments.

The account also follows the steadfastness of her companions, including Sanctus’s insistence that his Christian identity mattered more than the other answers demanded of him. Its heading dates the group’s suffering to about 172; the profile preserves the account as a shared witness rather than separating it into invented individual timelines.

Their family circumstances form part of the account’s testimony to steadfast faith. Felicitas distinguishes the suffering of childbirth from the suffering she will bear as a Christian, and both remain faithful when sentenced to death. The heading places their witness at about 201.

The account says he preached for about twenty years and was burned at St. Giles in 1145. It then follows his disciple Henry of Toulouse and the persecution of those who continued their teaching. The joined narrative supplies the relationship between the two teachers.

title: The Zürich baptisms

date.label: 21 January 1525
date.basis: Date in the cited MWC history and supplied overview 9361-G.

summary: On 21 January 1525, Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock at a gathering associated with Felix Manz in Zürich. This is a central starting point for Swiss Anabaptist history.
paragraphs: Bible study in Zürich led Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, George Blaurock, and their companions to seek a fellowship shaped by the New Testament. Their conviction that baptism should follow personal faith brought them into conflict with the city’s requirement that infants be baptized. The supplied overview describes the council’s order to conform or leave.

On 21 January 1525 the believers gathered in the home associated with Manz’s mother. After prayer, Blaurock asked Grebel to baptize him upon his confession of faith. Blaurock then baptized others in the gathering. The act joined the outward sign to a deliberate commitment to follow Christ together.

The gathering became a defining beginning of the Swiss Brethren. Its consequences can be followed through the lives of the three men: Manz’s imprisonment and death at Zürich, Blaurock’s continued preaching into Tyrol, and Grebel’s place in the first fellowship. The linked first-century source passages show the biblical pattern of teaching, faith, and baptism to which they appealed.

title: Felix Manz and the cost of conviction

date.label: 5 January 1527
date.basis: Date in the cited later history and supplied overview; Martyrs’ Mirror itself gives 1526.

summary: Felix Manz was drowned in Zürich on 5 January 1527. His story is central to the memory of persecution among the Swiss Brethren.
paragraphs: Felix Manz helped form the Zürich fellowship and continued teaching the baptism of believers under increasing pressure from the city authorities. His execution by drowning in the Limmat on 5 January 1527 became an early and enduring witness in the history of the Swiss Brethren.

Martyrs’ Mirror preserves more than the circumstances of his death. Its account, under the spelling Felix Mantz, includes an admonition calling believers to repentance, faith, love, and mercy. Manz contrasts that life with the hatred and coercion of teachers who appeal to the authorities to put their opponents to death.

The supplied book’s heading and narrative give 1526. The later history and the supplied overview give 5 January 1527, which is the date used for this event. The original account remains unchanged and directly accessible, so the difference is preserved with the testimony rather than silently removed.

title: The Schleitheim Articles

date.label: 24 February 1527
date.basis: The supplied overview 9361-K gives the gathering date; the cited historical document preserves the seven articles.

summary: The Schleitheim Articles set out seven points of agreement for a gathered Anabaptist community, including baptism, communion, church discipline, and refusal of the sword.
paragraphs: The brethren who met at Schleitheim in 1527 sought agreement about the life of the gathered church. The document associated with Michael Sattler was a brotherly union, written to strengthen believers and give practical expression to their common commitment to Christ.

Its seven articles connect baptism upon repentance and faith with discipline, communion, separation from evil, and the care of the congregation by its shepherds. They also reject the use of the sword by Christ’s followers and the swearing of oaths. The articles repeatedly appeal to Scripture and treat belief and conduct as inseparable.

Martyrs’ Mirror’s account of Sattler shows how these convictions came under examination. The charges against him included his teaching on baptism, the Lord’s Supper, oaths, and resistance by force. His prison letter to the church at Horb carries the same concern for a faithful, orderly, loving fellowship through a time of danger.

title: Community of goods in Moravia

date.basis: Shared-goods episode in the supplied overview 9362-F and Hutterite institutional history.

summary: A community of Anabaptist refugees in Moravia began sharing their possessions. This practice became a defining feature of Hutterite life.
paragraphs: Anabaptists who had found refuge near Nikolsburg faced a division over participation in war and the payment of war taxes. Those who held that Christ’s followers should refuse violence left rather than defend the settlement by force. Their departure made the provision of food, shelter, and other necessities an immediate concern.

In 1528 the group gathered what they had brought with them and placed it on a cloak for common use. The supplied overview and the Hutterite history present this act of mutual provision as a beginning of community of goods, following the shared life described in Acts.

The believers settled at Austerlitz and were joined by further refugees. Jakob Hutter later helped organize and lead the communities. The event therefore connects the debate at Nikolsburg, the practical care of displaced people, and a form of shared Christian life that became central to the Hutterite tradition.

title: Jakob Hutter’s witness

date.label: 25 February 1536

summary: Jakob Hutter was executed in Innsbruck in 1536. His leadership and organization helped give the Hutterite tradition its lasting name.
paragraphs: Jakob Hutter’s leadership linked the persecuted believers of Tyrol with communities of refuge in Moravia. Martyrs’ Mirror describes Jacob Huter as a teacher and overseer whose people joined the Moravian church, and records his role in sending ministers to serve there.

The Hutterite history relates that he was captured on a missionary journey to Austria and burned at Innsbruck on 25 February 1536. The supplied overview places his death after years of organizing refugees, addressing differences, and strengthening the shared life of the brethren.

His death did not end the communities he had served. Their later history retained his name and continued through periods of growth, displacement, and renewal. The linked source account provides the earlier Tyrolean and Moravian setting, while the institutional history supplies the execution date and place.

title: Dirk Willems saves his pursuer

date.label: 1569; sentence dated 16 May
date.basis: Rescue year and sentence date in the preserved Martyrs’ Mirror account; the day of the rescue is not assigned.

summary: Martyrs’ Mirror recounts how Dirk Willems turned back to rescue a pursuer who had fallen through the ice. He was recaptured and later executed.
paragraphs: Dirk Willems fled across the ice at Asperen in 1569 while an officer pursued him. When the officer broke through, Dirk turned back and helped him out of the water. Martyrs’ Mirror makes the rescue the decisive moment of the account: he chose to save the life of the man who was trying to capture him.

The rescued officer wished to let him go, but the burgomaster ordered him to remember his oath. Dirk was seized again, imprisoned, and condemned to death. The book preserves a copy of the town’s sentence, dated 16 May 1569, alongside the narrative of his suffering.

The illustration depicts Dirk reaching toward his pursuer in the water. Read together with the account and sentence, it presents mercy toward an enemy as a costly act of discipleship. The rescue itself is dated to the year; the surviving sentence supplies the precise May date.

title: Hans Landis and the Swiss persecution

date.label: September 1614
date.basis: Month and year stated in the principal Martyrs’ Mirror account.

summary: The account of Hans Landis in Martyrs’ Mirror shows that persecution of Swiss Anabaptists continued into the seventeenth century.
paragraphs: Hans Landis continued to teach and care for believers when the Zürich authorities ordered him to stop. Martyrs’ Mirror presents his ministry as the feeding of people hungry for the word of God and explains his refusal to abandon them through the duty to obey God.

The account follows his arrest, removal to Solothurn, release through the assistance of friends, and a later arrest at Zürich. When he would not give up his convictions, he was sentenced to death and beheaded in September 1614. The authorities represented the punishment as a response to disobedience; the book records it as suffering for his faith.

A following section preserves a later letter from an observer who remembered his death. Bringing the narrative and recollection together gives a fuller account of a named minister and shows that persecution of the Swiss Brethren continued well into the seventeenth century.

title: Preserving the memory: Martyrs’ Mirror

date.label: 1660: publication
date.basis: Publication year on the supplied overview; linked authorial addresses are dated 1659.

summary: Thieleman J. van Braght’s collection preserved accounts of Christian witnesses and Anabaptist martyrs, along with letters, confessions, and reflections.
paragraphs: Thieleman J. van Braght’s Martyrs’ Mirror brought together accounts of Christian witness from the time of Christ through the sufferings of the Anabaptists. The work alternates teaching about baptism and faith with narratives of persecution, joining the beliefs of the church to the lives of those who held them.

Its letters, confessions, court records, and personal testimonies give the witnesses a voice beyond the account of their deaths. Van Braght’s addresses to fellow believers explain the purpose: to encourage a living faith expressed in love, obedience, and steadfastness. His valedictory is signed at Dort in 1659, before the 1660 publication milestone.

The supplied overview follows the book’s later illustrated and translated editions. This archive preserves the supplied English edition in full, including its original headings, page markers, and images, while linking its sections to named people, places, and events. The first-century and medieval accounts therefore remain part of the same navigable history as the later Anabaptist witnesses.

title: Hans de Ries

date.label: 1615: history of the martyrs
date.basis: Publication year documented by the Mennonite Encyclopedia; the profile also describes his wider ministry.

summary: Waterlander teacher and collector whose 1615 martyr history helped prepare the way for Martyrs’ Mirror.
paragraphs: Hans de Ries (1553–1638) was a Dutch Mennonite teacher associated with the Waterlanders. Baptized at De Rijp, he later served the congregation at Alkmaar and worked with other ministers on confessions of faith. He sought peace and cooperation among Mennonite groups divided over church practice.

He gathered reports and records of those who had suffered for their faith and encouraged others to contribute. In 1615 he published Historie der Martelaren, bringing a larger body of testimony together. His introduction urged the churches to learn love and peace from the witnesses whose suffering they remembered.

The work appeared in further editions and became an important foundation for Thieleman J. van Braght’s later collection. De Ries therefore connects the Waterlander story with the preservation of martyr accounts: the book inherited by later readers grew through the work of collectors, editors, and congregations as well as its best-known compiler.

title: Cornelis Ris

date.label: 1766 publication; 1773 recognition
date.basis: The 1766 confession and its 1773 recognition are documented in Mennonite confessional history; no unreadable chart date is inferred.

summary: The Hoorn minister whose 1766 confession circulated among Dutch and German Mennonite congregations.
paragraphs: Cornelis Ris (1717–1790), called Cornelius Ris on the supplied timeline, served as a Mennonite preacher at Hoorn from 1747 until his death. His best-known work was a detailed account of the faith, published at Hoorn in 1766 under the title De geloofsleere der waare Mennoniten of Doopsgezinden.

The confession contained thirty-six articles. In 1773 it was recognized by the society of Mennonite churches whose delegates met at the Zonist church in Amsterdam. This reception helped it circulate beyond the author’s own congregation; a German edition followed at Hamburg in 1776.

Its later use included instruction and discussion among North American Mennonites. A proposal to make it the General Conference’s official confession did not succeed, so its influence should be distinguished from formal adoption. The linked texts follow a particular minister and document through the churches that read and used them.

title: Christopher Dock

date.label: 1718–1771: documented teaching and death
date.basis: Dock’s institutional history places his arrival around 1714 and teaching at Skippack in 1718; 1714 is not treated as his birth year.

summary: Pennsylvania schoolmaster whose teaching, illustrated writing, and School Management joined learning with Christian formation.
paragraphs: Christopher Dock taught children in the Mennonite settlements of southeastern Pennsylvania. The school that bears his name places his arrival in America around 1714 and the beginning of his work at Skippack in 1718. The chart’s 1714–1771 caption therefore should not be read as a lifespan.

His school life joined reading and writing with Christian conduct. Decorated examples of handwriting served both as models and as rewards. His surviving account of school management describes attention to the needs of individual children, the responsibilities of the teacher, and the formation of habits of learning and godliness.

Dock wrote his Schul-Ordnung in 1750; it was published by Christopher Saur at Germantown in 1770. He died in 1771. His own writing, preserved in later editions, lets readers examine the daily practice of a Mennonite schoolmaster rather than relying only on the familiar image of him praying for his pupils.

title: Johann Cornies

date.label: 1817: agricultural society leadership
date.basis: The Mennonite Encyclopedia documents Cornies’s chairmanship by 1817; the date describes that activity, not his birth.

summary: Molotschna leader associated with agricultural improvement, settlement development, and the society marked on the timeline in 1817.
paragraphs: The timeline’s Cornies is Johann Cornies (1789–1848), a leader in the Mennonite settlements of the Russian Empire. His family moved from the Danzig region in 1804, spent time at Chortitza, and then settled in the Molotschna colony. Farming and trade gave him the means to undertake wider agricultural projects.

By 1817 he had been appointed chairman of a society promoting tree planting, horticulture, silk production, and vine growing, later known as an agricultural association. His work included livestock breeding, crop experiments, irrigation, and nurseries that supplied trees to the settlements. These activities help explain the chart’s agricultural-improvement marker.

His influence reached beyond an individual farm into the organization of colonial life, backed by government authority. The Mennonite Archives of Ontario preserves a Cornies fonds concerning the later division of his estate. Its records and the biographical history connect the name on the chart to a documented person, community, and body of surviving evidence.

title: Claas Epp Jr.

date.label: 1880–1882: trek to Central Asia
date.basis: Mennonite biographical and archival sources identify the 1880 leader as the younger Claas Epp and trace settlement at Ak-Mechet in 1882.

summary: The younger Claas Epp led an eastward migration in 1880 while expecting a place of refuge before Christ’s return.
paragraphs: Claas Epp Jr. (1838–1913) is the leader associated with the timeline’s 1880 trek. He must be distinguished from his father, also named Claas Epp, who helped lead a migration from Prussia to the Volga region in 1853. The younger Epp grew up in the Am Trakt settlement.

As changes to Russian privileges brought uncertainty about military obligations, he taught that believers should seek refuge in the east in preparation for Christ’s return. In 1880 he led a group toward Central Asia. The migration divided, and his smaller group eventually settled at Ak-Mechet in the Khanate of Khiva in 1882.

Epp’s predictions of Christ’s return did not come to pass, and his authority over the group later broke down. His history is therefore an account of a particular leader, expectation, and migration within Russian Mennonite experience. The archival and biographical references identify the people and route without turning the chart’s brief trek marker into a general movement of all Mennonites.

title: Daniel Hege

date.label: 1861–1862: itinerant ministry
date.basis: The 1861 Reiseprediger appointment is documented by Mennonite Historian; his death on 30 November 1862 is recorded in the Mennonite Encyclopedia.

summary: An early General Conference minister who traveled among congregations to encourage fellowship, mission, and education.
paragraphs: Daniel Hege (1826–1862) was born in the Palatinate and immigrated to the United States in 1851. After further study and work in schools and congregations, he became pastor at Summerfield, Illinois, in 1859. His concern extended to the scattered churches that were forming the General Conference.

At the 1861 conference at Wadsworth he took part in establishing the new organization and was elected secretary. He was also appointed as its traveling preacher, or Reiseprediger. His journeys brought preaching and pastoral visits to congregations and families while encouraging cooperation, mission, publications, and support for a training school.

Hege’s fundraising travels helped prepare the way for the Wadsworth school, but he did not live to see that work fully develop. Returning ill from Iowa, he died of typhoid fever at Summerfield on 30 November 1862. His short ministry links the conference’s formation to the practical work of visiting, teaching, and gathering support across distance.

title: John Fretz Funk

date.label: 1864 beginnings; 1867 move to Elkhart
date.basis: Mennonite Church USA Archives dates the publishing business to Chicago in 1864 and its relocation to Elkhart in 1867.

summary: Publisher and Mennonite leader whose Elkhart work circulated periodicals, historical books, and practical help for immigrants.
paragraphs: John Fretz Funk (1835–1930), named John Funk on the supplied chart, came from Bucks County, Pennsylvania. He worked as a teacher and then in Chicago’s lumber trade before beginning a publishing business in January 1864. He moved himself and the business to Elkhart, Indiana, in 1867.

His periodicals included Herald of Truth and Mennonitische Rundschau. He also published editions of Menno Simons’s writings and Martyrs’ Mirror, making the older witness available to new generations. Printing became a means of connecting dispersed congregations through teaching, news, discussion, and shared memory.

Funk also assisted Mennonites migrating from the Russian Empire in the 1870s through the Mennonite Board of Guardians. His surviving papers at Mennonite Church USA Archives include correspondence, diaries, and other records of this wider work. The Elkhart marker thus belongs to a life of publishing, church leadership, and material assistance, rather than merely the opening of a print shop.
